edits.old: Inference for compound hashed shard keys: MongoDB defines the compound form as an index with one hashed key and other ordinary ordered keys, while its index-type manual says hashed indexes cannot cover queries. The compound hashed index should therefore be treated as non-covering even when ordinary fields match the query and projection. The cited server test directly checks only a single-field hashed shard key, not this compound case. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20)
edits.new: MongoDB defines a compound hashed index as a compound index with a single hashed field, whose hash is used along with the other fields as the shard key. The hashed-index manual says hashed indexes can't cover a query; it does not separately address the compound case, so treating compound hashed indexes as non-covering is an inference. The cited server test checks only a single-field {_id: "hashed"} shard key. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/hashed-sharding/ ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-hashed/

edits.old: With a single-field hashed shard key, equality matches can target one shard; hashing preserves distribution for monotonically changing values but removes original-value range locality, so a range predicate cannot use the hashed index and may broadcast to multiple shards. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-08-04)
edits.new: With a single-field hashed shard key, mongos can target queries with equality matches to a single shard. Hashing gives a more even distribution (hashed keys suit monotonically changing fields), but documents with close shard key values are unlikely to share a chunk or shard, so mongos is more likely to broadcast a ranged query. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/hashed-sharding/
